rv.q: Zeldin’s script dives from black comedy to horror, while his staging gives us a brilliant compound of the ordinary and the eerie.
Menzies and D'Arcy, the entrancingly stubborn elder daughter, deliver a climax that sent a series of collective gasps of shock through the audience on the night I went.
All these quibbles can’t take away from the vivid family dynamic that Zeldin and his cast create here.
It is an accomplishment that this drama generates gasping shocks with such an ancient story.

The urn of ashes is constantly being decanted into a Ziploc bag in a tug-of-war that’s partly a farce, with Jerry Killick providing laughs as the sleazebag family friend. The shock revelation I can’t spoil. But while it’s compelling to watch, it’s got a feel of wilful obscurity and it lacks the stark, epic quality of the classic it vaguely recycles.
It’s a muddled showing from Zeldin the writer.
The malnourished torpor appealed to the depressive masochist in me, but needn't detain better-adjusted theatre-goers.
The Other Place does a simple thing in a sophisticated way.
It is strange, twisted yet terribly feasible, and utterly gripping.
Chris undergoes a three-part personality shift – reasonable patriarch to raging bully to a man weakened by his own misguided sexuality – that, in the space of a day, is not entirely believable.

Zeldin has the basis of a really interesting family drama and the tensions that emerge from the loss of a family member, but The Other Place feels slight and needs more time to establish the characters and make their desire to be free of their grief more tangible.
The 80 minutes fly by, and that goes to show how gripping this slick, modernised spin on Antigone is.
But for all the skill and effort, and the insistence that it’s based on Sophocles’ Antigone, it doesn’t fly however hard they all pedal.

cn.t: Zeldin's contemporary Antigone adaptation earns praise for D'Arcy and Menzies' searing performances and atmospheric intensity, though critics split on whether the Greek tragedy translates effectively to a modern family psychodrama.
